summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory in which local legislation governs criminal and family law. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 code of practice on single-sex services do not apply of their own force here; both can be extended to the territory only by Order in Council.

Private consensual same-sex conduct is legal, but the change was made by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council rather than by Anguilla's own House of Assembly. Wire coverage of the decision in January 2001 records that the court ordered decriminalisation across five British territories after each local legislature declined to act, and that religious leaders protested the ruling. Anguilla itself never carried the prohibition in the same statutory form as the neighbouring islands.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguillan law. Commercial operators selling destination weddings on the island state this plainly while marketing their venues to same-sex couples, so any ceremony booked there is symbolic and confers no legal status.

A queer family visiting in June 2023 described the stay as uneventful. The territory has roughly 15,000 residents across 35 square miles, and public LGBT life is muted rather than visible: there are no community organisations, no dedicated venues and no Pride event. A small number of hotels market themselves to gay travellers, and same-sex wedding packages are sold on the promise of a friendly, relaxed atmosphere.
tangentialFactors:
Anguilla's decriminalisation was not an isolated act. The same Privy Council ruling in January 2001 ordered the repeal of laws against private consensual same-sex conduct in the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and Turks and Caicos as well, in every case after the local legislature had refused to move. The pattern across these five territories is of reform delivered from London over the head of elected members, accompanied by protest from religious leaders.

That imposed origin shapes what a visitor sees on the ground. Reporting from 2023 links the absence of an 'out and proud' public culture directly to the colonial legacy of the change rather than to any current legal pressure, and the territory's small population reinforces it. The practical picture for a trans or queer visitor is therefore a place where same-sex conduct carries no legal risk but where visible community infrastructure is close to absent.

The United Kingdom framework sits at a distance from the territory in the other direction as well. Equality protections that a visitor might assume follow from British sovereignty, including the single-sex-services code, require a separate extension order before they have any effect in Anguilla.
localsOnly:
Anguilla's House of Assembly declined to repeal its own prohibition, and the change was imposed by the Privy Council in January 2001 alongside four other British territories. Religious leaders publicly protested the ruling at the time, and the reform is understood locally as something chosen in London rather than in the House of Assembly.

Residents live with roughly 15,000 people on 35 square miles and no organised LGBT community presence: no associations, no venues, no annual Pride. Social visibility is low by circumstance as much as by choice, and the small number of hotels catering to gay travellers operates as a commercial niche rather than as a community fixture.

For residents, as for visitors, same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. Couples can hold ceremonies on the island, but the resulting status is not recognised under Anguillan law, which affects local families as well as those arriving for a wedding.
outOfScopeNotes:
The date of decriminalisation is unresolved in the sources held here. A first-person account published in June 2023 gives the change as 2000, while the contemporaneous Associated Press report of the Privy Council ruling is dated 5 January 2001. Both are reproduced above without reconciliation.

No source in this inventory addresses gender recognition: whether Anguilla has a process for changing legal gender, what documents a trans visitor may present at the border, or whether immigration or outbound screening questions a traveller's gender marker. Entry and visa requirements for trans passport holders are likewise not sourced here.

Also not sourced: any hate-crime or aggravated-offence provision with a gender identity component, the enforcement record of the 2001 decriminalisation order, access to gender-affirming healthcare on the island, and the legal position on restroom or facility access. Each of these remains unresolved rather than answered in either direction.
